source_title: Why You Should Know Marlborough (Beyond Sauvignon Blanc)
newsletter_intro:
Marlborough got famous for Sauvignon Blanc, but that’s only part of the story. If you’ve only ever stopped there, I’d love to show you what else the region does well.

There’s Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Riesling, and even the little details that make the sub-regions worth paying attention to. Let’s get into it.

instagram_reel.script:
Everybody knows Marlborough for Sauvignon Blanc. Fair. It’s iconic.

But that region has a whole other side people sleep on. Marlborough Pinot Noir is lighter and more elegant. Pinot Gris brings more weight and texture. And Marlborough Riesling? Underrated gem.

What I also love is how much the sub-regions matter. Wairau Valley, Awatere Valley, the Southern Valleys — same region, different vibe.

So next time you’re shopping, don’t just grab the Savi B. Look a little wider and see what Marlborough is really doing.

tiktok.script:
Okay, quick wine check: Marlborough is famous for Sauvignon Blanc, yes — but that is not the whole story.

Marlborough Pinot Noir is a thing, and it tends to be lighter and more elegant than the richer styles you might expect elsewhere. Pinot Gris is also doing good work there, with more body and texture. And Marlborough Riesling? Very underrated.

What makes the region interesting is that the sub-regions shift the style too. Wairau Valley, Awatere Valley, Southern Valleys — they don’t all taste the same.

So next time you see a Marlborough bottle, don’t autopilot to just one grape. There’s more to try.

linkedin.post:
Marlborough has earned its global reputation through Sauvignon Blanc, and for good reason. It remains one of the most recognizable and reliable wine styles coming out of New Zealand.

But the region’s story is broader than one iconic grape. Marlborough Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, and Riesling all deserve more attention, especially as more drinkers and buyers look for regions with depth, range, and consistency.

What makes Marlborough especially compelling is the influence of its sub-regions. The Wairau Valley, Awatere Valley, and Southern Valleys each shape wines differently, adding nuance that trade and consumers alike can talk about with more confidence.

For anyone building a more complete understanding of New Zealand wine, Marlborough is an easy place to start — and an even better place to keep exploring.

It’s a reminder that strong regions are rarely one-dimensional.
